messages.content:
Two things beyond what the implementer's brief covers:

1. tests/probe.test.ts (a debug dump writing PROBE_OUT.txt) is in the repo and is the direct cause of the failing gates: `npm run typecheck` fails with "tests/probe.test.ts(2,31): error TS2307: Cannot find module 'node:fs'" (tsconfig has no node types / @types/node), lint fails on its unused `toggleFlag` import and explicit `any` (tests/probe.test.ts:3,5), and vitest picks it up as a test file. It is not part of any task I can see — it looks like leftover debugging. Removing it (and PROBE_OUT.txt) should clear the typecheck/lint/test gates.

2. On review, tests/engine.test.ts [R18] (lines 271-342) appears to fail even in isolation: the layout has mines at row 1 cols 0-3 and the click is (3,2), which is adjacent to mine (1,2), so reveal only reveals that single numbered cell — no flood. `lastRevealed` is then just [(3,2):0], every distance equals its Manhattan distance, and line 341 `expect(differsFromGeometric).toBe(true)` fails. The "winding zero corridor" the test describes never gets revealed because the clicked cell isn't a zero cell. A click on a zero cell (e.g. (3,0)) would actually exercise the corridor.

The premise "the engine is fine and not yours to change" is contradicted by the code. src/game/engine.ts:316-318 calls placeMines on EVERY first reveal when status==='ready' — including games created from a `layout` — with mineCount = game.mines (engine.ts:305-307 sets mines=true on random candidates; no seed for layout games so it uses Math.random, engine.ts:196-198). So revealing a 1-mine layout game adds a second random mine. Evidence the implementer's own probe captured this: PROBE_OUT.txt line 7-12 shows `reveal(2,2) status=playing flags=0` and a board with TWO M's (at 0,0 and 4,3) for a 1-mine layout. Consequences: the [R20] test's `expect(flagCount(g)).toBe(1)` (tests/engine.test.ts:386) fails whenever the extra mine is not re-placed on itself (~13/14 of runs; harness recorded exactly this failure), and R14's "mines never move / board is exactly that grid" is violated by the engine while tests/engine.test.ts:170-172 only asserts two specific cells are still mines — a weaker claim that passes despite the violation. No test-only fix can make [R20] pass deterministically; this needs either an engine change (skip placeMines when a layout was given) or the requirement re-scoped. Also note tests/probe.test.ts (debug artifact writing PROBE_OUT.txt) is what breaks npm run typecheck/lint (TS2307 node:fs, unused 'toggleFlag', explicit any) and should be deleted along with PROBE_OUT.txt.

messages.subject: Two e2e failures are product bugs in the page layer (not test errors)
messages.content:
My e2e suite (playwright.config.ts + e2e/minesweeper.spec.ts) is otherwise green: 27/29 pass. The two failures are genuine product defects in files I'm scoped out of (src/page/*, src/main.ts — hidden from me), so I can't fix them here.

1) R31 "changing #difficulty starts a new game of that size" — the page persists the choice (localStorage minesweeper.difficulty=intermediate confirmed) but does NOT start a new game live: after selectOption('intermediate') the board stays 81 cells (9x9); it only becomes 256 (16x16) after page.reload(). Spec R31 requires the change to immediately start a new game of that size. Likely in src/main.ts / src/page/board.ts difficulty-change handler — it updates persistence but not the live board.

2) R26/R34 loss "the mine that lost the game also has data-exploded=true" — with multiple mines, data-exploded lands on the FIRST mine in iteration order, not the clicked one. Probed: layout '.*...,*....' (mines at (0,1) and (1,0)); clicking the mine at (0,1) → (0,1) gets data-state="mine" but NO data-exploded; instead (1,0) gets data-exploded="true". Single-mine boards are correct. Root cause is in src/game/engine.ts toLost() (lines 292-299): it reveals all mines but never records which one was hit, so the page can't mark the exploded one — it defaults to the first mine. Either the engine should expose the hit cell, or the page should track the clicked coordinate and mark that specific mine.

Both tests assert exactly what the spec quotes; I have not weakened them. They will pass once the page/engine is fixed.

R45 (reveal ripple) is not implemented in the page: on ?board=*....,.....,.....,.....,..... clicking (3,3), every one of the 24 revealed cells animates with delay=0 (CSSTransition, duration 120ms), and all data-state flips land at the same frame (t≈116ms). Spec section 5 / R45 requires each cell to start `distance × step` after the input with a fixed step of 15–40 ms (engine already exposes lastRevealed with per-cell distance — src/game/engine.ts Revealed interface), so cells at different distances must visibly ripple outward. The page is ignoring the distance and applying one undelayed transition to all cells. Likely in src/page/animation.ts / src/page/board.ts: it should set a per-cell delay (e.g. transition-delay or animation-delay = distance × step) from game.lastRevealed. My R45 test now asserts staggering (distinct delays, 15–40 ms gaps between consecutive distinct delays, every start ≤ 1000 ms) per the requirement and correctly fails against the current build. It will pass once the page staggers by distance.

requirements.quote: TypeScript in strict mode, built with Vite, unit-tested with Vitest, end-to-end tested with Playwright, linted with ESLint.
**No runtime dependencies.** `package.json` may have `devDependencies` only; the shipped game is your own code.
`npm run build` | type-checks, then writes the static site to `dist/`
`npm run typecheck` | `tsc --noEmit` (or equivalent)
`npm run lint` | ESLint over the source and tests, no warnings allowed
`npm test` | the unit tests, once (not watch mode)
`npm run test:e2e` | the Playwright tests, against the production build
`npm run check` | typecheck, lint, test and build, stopping at the first failure

opening `dist/index.html` straight from disk (double-clicked, a `file://` address, no server at all) gives a playable game. A browser refuses to load separate script or style files for a page opened that way, so they belong inside the page.
The built site must also work from **any path** on a static server — at `/` and at a sub-path such as `/games/minesweeper/` — so any asset URLs are relative.
export const DIFFICULTIES: { beginner: { rows: 9; cols: 9; mines: 10 }; intermediate: { rows: 16; cols: 16; mines: 40 }; expert: { rows: 16; cols: 30; mines: 99 }; };
**Immutable.** No function changes the `Game` it is given. A call that changes nothing returns the very same object it was given.
`rows` and `cols` are integers from 5 to 50, and `mines` from 1 to `rows × cols − 9`. Anything else makes `createGame` throw a `RangeError`.
With `layout`, the board is exactly that grid: `rows`, `cols` and `mines` come from it (any given are ignored), mines never move, and `adjacent` is set from the start. The size rule still applies.

Without `layout`, mines are placed at the first `reveal`: exactly `mines` of them, never on the revealed cell or any of its neighbours. With a `seed`, the placement depends only on the seed, the board size and the first cell. Until placement every cell has `adjacent: 0` and `mine: false`.

`ready` until the first reveal, then `playing`; `lost` when a mine is revealed; `won` when every non-mine cell is revealed (flags are not needed). Once `won` or `lost`, every function returns the game unchanged.

If it has `adjacent: 0`, its neighbours are revealed too, and so on outward: the connected region of zero cells and the numbered cells bordering it (8-neighbour connectivity). Flagged cells are never revealed this way. ... Revealing a revealed or flagged cell changes nothing.

`lastRevealed` lists every cell the call revealed, each with its `distance`: 0 for the clicked cell, otherwise the fewest steps from the clicked cell to it, moving one neighbour at a time and passing only through revealed zero cells.
**Loss.** Revealing a mine reveals every mine, and the game is `lost`. Flags stay where they are.
**Win.** When the game is `won`, every mine is flagged.
`toggleFlag` flags or unflags a hidden cell; on a revealed cell it changes nothing. There may be more flags than mines.

`chord` on a revealed cell whose number equals the count of flagged neighbours reveals every hidden, unflagged neighbour, exactly as `reveal` would (flood included, and a wrong flag can lose the game). ... Otherwise `chord` changes nothing.
`lastRevealed` measures `distance` from the chorded cell, which is 0 but not itself newly revealed.
`minesLeft` is `mines` minus the number of flagged cells; it can be negative.

`#board` | `role="grid"`; contains one `role="row"` per row, each holding one `<button role="gridcell">` per cell; ... each row's cells side by side on one line, rows stacked top to bottom, so the cells of a column line up

each cell button | `data-row`, `data-col` (0-based); `data-state` is `hidden`, `flagged`, `revealed`, `mine` (a revealed mine) or `wrong-flag` (after a loss, a flag on a non-mine); the mine that lost the game also has `data-exploded="true"`; a revealed cell with `adjacent > 0` has that number as its text, otherwise no text; an `aria-label` that says the cell's position and state
`#status` | `data-status` is the game's status; its text tells the player what is going on
`#mines-left` | `minesLeft`, as text (`-2` when over-flagged)
`#timer` | whole seconds since the first reveal, as text; `0` before; stops when the game ends; never above `999`
requirements.not_tested: The 'never above 999' half of the #timer contract cannot be exercised in e2e without a 16-minute wait or a Date.now mock; the observable halves (0 before first reveal, stopped after win/loss) are e2e-tested and the cap is enforced in page code and verified by review.

requirements.quote: `#new-game` | a button: a fresh game of the same kind (same difficulty, or the same `?board`)
`#difficulty` | a `<select>` with options `beginner`, `intermediate`, `expert`; changing it starts a new game of that size; the choice is remembered across reloads
`#best-time` | the fastest win for the current board, in whole seconds, or `—` (an em dash) if there is none; kept across reloads
`#mute` | a button, `aria-pressed="true"` when muted; muted state is remembered across reloads; unmuted by default
**Mouse:** left click reveals; right click toggles a flag (no browser menu appears); left click on a revealed number chords.

**Keyboard:** the board is one Tab stop — exactly one cell has `tabindex="0"`, the rest `-1`. Arrow keys move focus between cells and stop at the edges. Enter or Space reveals the focused cell, or chords it if it is a revealed number; `F` toggles its flag. Focus is always visible.
**State is immediate.** Cell `data-state`, `#mines-left`, `#status` and the rest change in the same task as the input that changed them — never after an animation.
**Best times** are kept per board: per difficulty, and per `?board` value. A win is recorded when it beats the stored time.

`?board=` fixes the board: rows separated by `,`, each a string of `*` (mine) and `.` (safe) — `?board=*....,.....,.....,.....,.....`. The game uses that layout (rule 3), and `#new-game` starts it again.
`?seed=` with an integer makes a random game repeatable (rule 4), at the current difficulty.
With neither, the board is random at the remembered difficulty (beginner the first time).
Every sound is synthesised with the Web Audio API — no audio files.

Distinct sounds for: revealing one cell, a cascade (one reveal that opens more than one cell), placing a flag, removing a flag, a chord, an explosion (loss), and a win — the win is a short melody of at least three notes.
**No sound before the player acts:** no `AudioContext` is created before the first click or key press on the page.
**Muted means silent:** while muted, no sound starts at all.

**Reveal ripple.** Every newly revealed cell animates in (100–600 ms), starting `distance × step` after the input, with a fixed step of 15–40 ms, so a cascade ripples outward from the click. No cell starts later than 1000 ms after the input.
**Flag.** Placing a flag animates.
**Loss.** The exploded mine animates (a flash, a shake), and the other mines appear one after another rather than all at once.
**Win.** The board or the status celebrates.
**Reduced motion.** When the user prefers reduced motion, nothing animates and nothing transitions: no CSS animations, no CSS transitions, no Web Animations.
The work is done when npm run check passes, and npm run test:e2e passes against the production build, as separate gates.
The unit tests cover the rules in section 2; the end-to-end tests drive the page through a browser.
Pure logic: no DOM, no timers, no `Math.random` except as described for `seed`.
